practical_skills: Choosing a card by how you will use it

sections.skill: Explain how a credit card works: credit limit, revolving balance, and grace period

questions.prompt: Leo uses a credit card to buy a $90 jacket. What happens to his money right away?

choices.text: Nothing yet; he now owes the card issuer $90
$90 leaves his checking account immediately, as with a debit card
The store waits to be paid until Leo pays his bill
The jacket is free if he pays the minimum each month

questions.correct_answer: Nothing yet; he now owes the card issuer $90
questions.intro: A credit card lets you borrow up to a credit limit to make purchases. The card issuer pays the store, and you owe the issuer. Each month you get a statement and can pay the full balance or a smaller amount (at least the minimum). Any unpaid balance "revolves" to the next month, usually with interest.
questions.feedback: The issuer paid the store; Leo now owes the issuer $90.

questions.prompt: Ben's card offers a grace period on purchases. He makes only purchases (no cash advances or balance transfers) and pays the full statement balance by the due date every month. How much interest does he pay on purchases?

choices.text: The full APR on every purchase
Half the APR, because he pays on time
$25 a month, the minimum payment

questions.intro: Most cards offer a grace period on purchases: if you pay the full statement balance by the due date, you are not charged interest on those purchases. Grace periods usually do not apply to cash advances. The law requires statements to be sent at least 21 days before the due date. Carrying a balance usually ends the grace period until the card is paid in full again.
questions.feedback: With a purchase grace period and full, on-time payment, no purchase interest is charged.

misconceptions.D: Confuses the minimum payment with interest

questions.prompt: Which statement describes "revolving" credit?

choices.text: You borrow one fixed amount and repay it on a schedule
You can only use it once, then the account closes
The balance is paid automatically by the bank
You can borrow, repay, and borrow again up to a limit

questions.correct_answer: You can borrow, repay, and borrow again up to a limit
questions.intro: Credit comes in two main forms. Installment credit (car loans, student loans) is one amount repaid in fixed payments. Revolving credit (credit cards, lines of credit) can be used again and again up to a limit, with payments that change with the balance.
questions.feedback: Credit cards are revolving: available credit returns as you repay.

questions.prompt: Jada is 19, has no income, and has no savings or other assets of her own. She applies for a credit card. Under federal law, what does she need?

choices.text: A cosigner or joint applicant 21 or older
Only a school ID, because students get automatic approval
Nothing; anyone over 18 must be approved
A parent's permission slip signed at school

questions.correct_answer: A cosigner or joint applicant 21 or older
questions.intro: The Credit CARD Act says applicants under 21 must show independent income or assets enough to make the minimum payments, or have a cosigner or joint applicant who is at least 21 and able to pay, if the issuer allows that.
questions.feedback: With no independent income or assets, she needs a qualified cosigner or joint applicant 21 or older (where the issuer allows one).

questions.prompt: A card has a 24% purchase APR. If Kai carries a $500 balance for a whole month, about how much interest is charged (monthly rate = APR ÷ 12)?
questions.intro: A credit card's APR is its yearly interest rate. Interest for about a month ≈ balance × (APR ÷ 12). (Many cards actually figure interest daily.)

questions.prompt: Two cards, both with a grace period on purchases: Card A 18% APR, $0 annual fee; Card B 15% APR, $95 annual fee. Ana uses the card only for purchases and pays the full statement balance on time every month. Which costs her less?

choices.text: Card B, because 15% is lower than 18%
They cost the same
Card B, because annual fees are refunded
Card A, because she pays no interest

questions.correct_answer: Card A, because she pays no interest
questions.intro: The best card depends on how you use it. If you keep a purchase grace period by always paying in full on time, the APR rarely matters, but fees do.
questions.feedback: Paying in full on time means no purchase interest, so the $95 fee is the only cost difference.

misconceptions.A: Ignores that she pays no interest

questions.prompt: A cash advance is…

choices.text: borrowing cash against your credit card
withdrawing your own savings with a debit card
a free bonus paid by the card issuer
a refund of a returned purchase

questions.correct_answer: borrowing cash against your credit card
questions.intro: A cash advance means using your credit card to get cash (at an ATM or bank). It is borrowing. Cash advances usually have a fee, a higher APR, and no grace period: interest starts right away.
questions.feedback: A cash advance is a loan of cash from your card issuer.
